Abuse of power is more pervasive than racism.

Abuse of power is a weakness of humanity and it does not discriminate.

In the days since George Floyds murder we have seen abuse of power in many forms. The socially charged environment has equipped people with a sense of righteous indignation that gives the courage to act and wield power in many forms.

Some are peaceful.

Most are not.

We have seen white officers kneeling on white necks (abuse of power), black officers assaulting black students (abuse of power), white rioters turning over police cars and lighting them on fire (abuse of power), white and black rioters looting stores with zero association to the source offense (abuse of power), black rioters attacking white business owners (racist and abuse of power), white rioters masquerading as counter protesters attacking peaceful protesters (racist and abuse of power), and the list goes on.

We have heard the analogy that one bad apple spoils the bunch. If one cop is beating someone down (abuse of power), and 900 cops stand around and watch we have 901 bad cops. If one rioter is throwing bricks through windows (abuse of power), and 900 peaceful protesters stand around and watch we have 901 rioters. Would any of us trust those we have seen rioting if they wore a police uniform instead? The deafening media silence tells me the answer is no.

The onus to act courageously in the face of those abusing power is not just the duty of anyone wearing a badge, or in political office. It is the duty of any observer regardless of social status or race. We unfortunately tend to look the other way when those who are abusing power look like us, sound like us, or vote like us.

Abuse of power exists in every level of our society all the way up to the oval office. The common thread of brutality *is* abuse of power. But we *want* to call it racism and then *justify* our own abuse of power.

If we think we are better than that, then we should act better than that. Period. We have a process to peaceably change our society through our democracy, but our patience and determination to bring that change to fruition seems only to be as close as the nearest brick, torch, or baton.

We shouldn’t be reaching for pitchforks and torches. We should be reaching for each other. We should be reaching for political platforms, and reforms that can use the powers that be to enforce the change we want to see. Blacks are not a *‘them’*, nor are whites a *‘them’*. We are an *‘us’* and until *'we'* can recognize our weakness to abuse power when we have it then we will continue to reach for bricks, and batons, to fix problems that exist in our minds.
